question: How high did oxygen go in the ACME gas-flame tests (BRE and CFI-G), and did any reach 30%?
claim: Yes: all 16 BRE test-day rows with oxygen data included a condition at 30% or more (up to 40%), and 230 of 333 CFI-G tests reached 30% or more (up to 85%).
summary_student: Gas flames were burned in space at oxygen levels above the one planned for a Moon base, much higher than normal air. Some of the highest values come from a special flame where oxygen is blown into the fuel, not from the air around it.
summary_professional: ACME BRE (PSI-20): O2 21–40% over 16 test-day rows, each including at least one condition at or above 30%. ACME CFI-G (PSI-159): XO2 12–85%, 230 of 333 tests at or above 30%; the highest values are inverse flames, where XO2 is the burner stream.

method.formula: For each investigation, the lowest and highest oxygen percentage over its tests that report oxygen, the number of those tests, and how many reached at least threshold_pct (o2_pct_max >= threshold_pct).

assumptions: Mole fraction and volume fraction are treated as equal (ideal gas).
A BRE row is one test day that lists several oxygen conditions; its highest condition is used.
limitations: BRE rows are test days, not single tests, so 16 counts days.
CFI-G inverse-flame oxygen is the burner stream, not the surrounding gas; it does not describe a breathable atmosphere.
These are gas flames; they say nothing about how solid materials burn.
warnings: PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data. Lunar and Mars conclusions are bounded by microgravity and Earth-gravity results only.

chart.idea: Range bars of the oxygen levels tested by BRE and CFI-G, with a dashed line at 30%.

visual_offer.footnote: Want a visual? I can draw a chart of the oxygen levels tested by BRE and CFI-G against the 30% lunar habitat target.
